content: Pelvic organ prolapse is a prevalent condition among women, with approximately 40% experiencing it at some point in their lives. This prevalence is expected to increase as the population ages. Women with prolapse often report symptoms such as a sensation of something descending into the vagina, pain, urinary and bowel dysfunction, and sexual difficulties. Treatment options for pelvic organ prolapse include surgery, pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), and the use of vaginal pessaries. Vaginal pessaries are mechanical devices designed to provide structural support to the vagina and reposition prolapsed organs into their correct anatomical location. Commonly used pessaries are made from materials such as polyvinyl chloride, polythene, silicone, or latex. They are widely utilized by clinicians, with many offering pessaries as a first-line treatment for prolapse. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of pessaries in managing pelvic organ prolapse and to summarize findings from economic evaluations of this intervention. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that involved pessaries as a treatment for prolapse. Four studies, involving a total of 478 women with varying stages of prolapse, were included. All studies were conducted in high-income countries. However, one trial had a very low participation rate, with only six out of 113 women consenting to randomization, and no data were available for these six participants. Due to the heterogeneity of the comparisons made in the trials, no meta-analysis could be performed. The studies did not report data on the resolution of prolapse symptoms or psychological outcomes. However, they did provide information on perceived improvement in prolapse symptoms. The trials were generally at high risk of performance bias due to the lack of blinding, but they had a low risk of selection bias. The certainty of the evidence was downgraded due to imprecision, as the trials involved a small number of participants. When comparing pessaries to no treatment, the evidence was very uncertain regarding their effect on perceived improvement in prolapse symptoms or the resolution of sexual problems after 12 months. One study involving 27 women reported a mean difference (MD) in questionnaire scores of -0.03 (95% confidence interval [CI] -0.61 to 0.55) for prolapse symptoms and an MD of -0.29 (95% CI -1.67 to 1.09) for sexual problems. No data were available on prolapse-specific quality of life or adverse events such as abnormal vaginal bleeding or new-onset voiding difficulties. When comparing pessaries to PFMT, the evidence was also uncertain. After 12 months, there was no clear difference in perceived improvement in prolapse symptoms (MD -9.60, 95% CI -22.53 to 3.33; 137 women; low-certainty evidence), prolapse-specific quality of life (MD -3.30, 95% CI -8.70 to 15.30; 116 women; low-certainty evidence), or resolution of sexual problems (MD -2.30, 95% CI -5.20 to 0.60; 48 women; low-certainty evidence). However, pessaries were associated with a significantly higher risk of adverse events compared to PFMT (relative risk [RR] 75.25, 95% CI 4.70 to 1205.45; 97 women; low-certainty evidence). Adverse events included increased vaginal discharge, urinary incontinence, and vaginal wall erosion or irritation. When comparing pessaries combined with PFMT to PFMT alone, the combination likely resulted in more women perceiving improvement in prolapse symptoms after 12 months (RR 2.15, 95% CI 1.58 to 2.94; 260 women; moderate-certainty evidence). The combination also likely improved prolapse-specific quality of life (median POPIQ score: pessary plus PFMT 0.3 [interquartile range (IQR) 0 to 22.2]; 132 women; PFMT alone 8.9 [IQR 0 to 64.9]; P = 0.02; moderate-certainty evidence). However, the combination may slightly increase the risk of abnormal vaginal bleeding compared to PFMT alone (RR 2.18, 95% CI 0.69 to 6.91; 260 women; low-certainty evidence). The evidence was uncertain regarding the effect of the combination on the risk of new-onset voiding difficulties (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.54 to 3.19; 189 women; low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, the evidence is uncertain regarding whether pessaries improve prolapse symptoms compared to no treatment or PFMT alone. However, the combination of pessaries and PFMT likely improves prolapse symptoms and prolapse-specific quality of life. Pessaries may be associated with an increased risk of adverse events compared to PFMT. Future research should focus on recruiting adequate numbers of participants and measuring clinically important outcomes, such as prolapse-specific quality of life and symptom resolution. Two economic evaluations were identified in the review: one assessed the cost-effectiveness of pessary treatment, expectant management, and surgical procedures, while the other compared pessary treatment to PFMT.
